photos.title: McKenzie River Forest
photos.blurb: Moss blankets a boulder and fallen logs above a shaded stream.
photos.story: Along the upper McKenzie River, water flows through ancient lava underground before reappearing at Tamolitch Blue Pool. The surrounding river corridor passes through old-growth forest.

photos.title: Meadow on the Obsidian Trail
photos.blurb: A rocky stream winds through golden grass beneath a snow-covered Cascade peak.
photos.story: The Obsidian Trail crosses the Three Sisters Wilderness, where glaciers and volcanic eruptions have shaped the landscape. North Sister last erupted about 55,000 years ago, while eruptions near South Sister occurred as recently as about 2,000 years ago.

photos.title: Multnomah Falls
photos.blurb: Umbrella-carrying visitors cross an arched bridge between two cascades.
photos.story: Benson Bridge was built in 1914, more than a decade before the waterfall’s historic lodge opened. Multnomah Falls descends 620 feet in two tiers.

photos.title: Wahkeena in the Fog
photos.blurb: A narrow forest path disappears into fog between dark tree trunks.
photos.story: Fog can supply water to a forest even when it is not raining. Tiny droplets collect on branches and leaves, then fall to the ground in a process called fog drip.

photos.title: Pool Beneath the Cliffs
photos.blurb: A shallow pool reflects evergreens at the foot of a broad slope of loose rock.
photos.story: The loose rock covering the hillside is called talus, formed as fragments break away from cliffs and collect below. The surrounding Obsidian Trail is named for the volcanic glass found along its route.

photos.title: Sahalie Falls
photos.blurb: White water plunges from a rocky ledge into a basin framed by moss.
photos.story: About 3,000 years ago, lava flowed into the upper McKenzie River valley. The end of one of those lava flows forms the ledge of Sahalie Falls.

photos.title: Descent into Silver Creek Canyon
photos.blurb: A mossy stone wall borders a descending path beside a fern-covered cliff.
photos.story: In the 1930s, the Civilian Conservation Corps began building trails, bridges and stone walls at Silver Falls State Park. The Canyon Trail takes hikers below the rim and behind several of the park’s waterfalls.

photos.title: Bend of the Crooked River
photos.blurb: A ribbon of green follows the Crooked River beneath towering golden cliffs.
photos.story: About 400,000 years ago, lava from Newberry Volcano diverted the Crooked River toward Smith Rock. The river gradually cut through the volcanic deposits, shaping the canyon seen today.

photos.title: The Spires of Smith Rock
photos.blurb: Jagged rock towers rise above a dry hillside against drifting clouds.
photos.story: Many of Smith Rock’s cliffs consist of tuff, rock made from volcanic ash and debris deposited by enormous eruptions nearly 30 million years ago. The park later became an important birthplace of modern American sport climbing.

photos.title: Snow Beyond the Spires
photos.blurb: A snow-covered mountain rises behind the jagged brown spires of Smith Rock.
photos.story: Moist air from the Pacific loses much of its water as it rises over the Cascades. The resulting rain shadow helps explain why Smith Rock’s high desert lies within sight of snow-covered mountains.

photos.title: A Forest Returning
photos.blurb: A rocky creek runs between bare tree trunks and green, densely vegetated banks.
photos.story: The 2017 Eagle Creek Fire burned much of the forest along the Multnomah–Wahkeena Loop. Standing dead trees, called snags, can provide nesting sites for woodpeckers as the forest recovers.
